identification.summary: APT16 is a China-based threat group that has run spear-phishing campaigns against Japanese and Taiwanese organizations [S2]. FireEye reported that between 26 November and 1 December 2015 known and suspected China-based APT groups, including APT16, sent spear-phishing emails to Japanese and Taiwanese organizations in the high-tech, government services, media and financial services sectors [S1][S4]. The lure documents exploited an Encapsulated PostScript (EPS) dict copy use-after-free flaw together with the Windows privilege escalation flaw CVE-2015-1701, and delivered either the IRONHALO downloader or the ELMER backdoor [S1][S4]. Press coverage of FireEye's research said Taiwanese news organizations and the opposition Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) were targeted ahead of Taiwan's January 2016 elections [S6][S7].
identification.firstObserved: FireEye's public reporting covers activity from 26 November to 1 December 2015 [S1][S4]. Earlier start dates that appear on secondary sites are not supported by the sources gathered.
identification.notes: Microsoft name: none found. APT16 and SVCMONDR do not appear in Microsoft's public threat-actor naming map (checked 2026-10-15) [S8]. Malpedia lists the aliases G0023 and SVCMONDR [S4]. APT16 is FireEye/Mandiant's designation, and MITRE tracks it as G0023 [S2]. Malpedia's Danti entry also lists ELMER as an associated malware family, so the tooling is not unique to this cluster [S4].

attribution.sponsor: China, a suspected state sponsor according to the CFR Cyber Operations Tracker [S5].
attribution.confidence: MITRE describes APT16 as 'China-based' [S2]. CFR lists China as the 'suspected state sponsor' [S5]. Press coverage reports that FireEye attributed the Taiwan activity to Chinese hackers [S6][S7]. No government attribution or indictment specific to APT16 was found.
attribution.basis: FireEye's December 2015 technical reporting on the EPS/CVE-2015-1701 spear-phishing campaigns [S1], which MITRE, Malpedia and CFR reuse [S2][S4][S5].

objectives: Espionage, classified as such by CFR [S5]. In the Taiwan campaign the reported aim was to obtain information on opposition (DPP) policies and speeches ahead of the January 2016 presidential and legislative elections [S6][S7].

targeting.notes: CFR files the target category as private sector [S5]. The 2015 reporting describes several China-based groups in the same window, so not every targeted sector necessarily belongs to APT16 alone [S1][S4].

capabilities.summary: Spear-phishing with malicious Microsoft Word documents that chain an EPS use-after-free exploit with CVE-2015-1701 for local privilege escalation [S1][S4]. The documents dropped IRONHALO, a downloader, or ELMER, a backdoor [S1][S4]. MITRE describes ELMER as a non-persistent, proxy-aware HTTP backdoor written in Delphi that can list directories and running processes [S3]. APT16 has compromised otherwise legitimate sites and used them as staging servers for second-stage payloads [S2]. In the Taiwan activity, emails reportedly used the lure subject 'DPP's Contact Information Update' [S6][S7].

campaigns.name: EPS / CVE-2015-1701 spear-phishing against Japan and Taiwan
campaigns.summary: From 26 November to 1 December 2015, spear-phishing emails carrying Word documents with the EPS exploit and CVE-2015-1701 hit Japanese and Taiwanese high-tech, government-services, media and financial organizations, delivering IRONHALO or ELMER.

campaigns.name: Targeting of Taiwanese media and the DPP before the 2016 election
campaigns.summary: Coverage of FireEye's research reports phishing of Taiwanese news organizations with a 'DPP's Contact Information Update' lure, seeking information on opposition policies and speeches before the January 2016 elections.

diamond.adversary: China-based group; China is the suspected state sponsor (CFR) [S2][S5].
diamond.capability: Weaponized Word documents (an EPS use-after-free exploit plus CVE-2015-1701), the IRONHALO downloader and the ELMER Delphi HTTP backdoor [S1][S3][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised legitimate websites used as staging servers for second-stage payloads; HTTP command and control for ELMER [S2][S3].
diamond.victim: Japanese and Taiwanese government-services, financial, media and high-tech organizations; Taiwan's DPP and news outlets [S1][S5][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Intelligence collection on Taiwanese domestic politics ahead of the January 2016 presidential and legislative elections [S6][S7].
diamond.technology: Unpatched Microsoft Office EPS handling and Windows privilege escalation (CVE-2015-1701) on victim endpoints [S1][S4].

gaps: FireEye's primary report 'The EPS Awakens' (2015-12-16) could not be opened (host unreachable). Details come from search excerpts and from Malpedia/MITRE quotations of it. 'The EPS Awakens Part 2', which MITRE also cites, was not reviewed.

The MITRE ATT&CK, Malpedia, CFR, SCMP and Security Affairs pages could not be fetched directly. Their content and dates come from search-result excerpts. The CFR entry date (2016-12) and the press dates (2015-12) need checking.
No Microsoft designation exists for APT16 in Microsoft's public naming map, so it may be untracked or merged without public disclosure.

The FireEye 2015 reporting covers several China-based groups in the same window. Which victims and sectors belong specifically to APT16 rather than other groups is not clear from the sources gathered.
A reported compromise of DPP staff email accounts appears only in secondary press excerpts. Whether it was APT16 activity is unverified.
Kaspersky's 2016 'CVE-2015-2545: overview of current threats' is an existing record reference that may mention SVCMONDR. It could not be retrieved or checked.
No public reporting on APT16 activity after 2015 was found, so its current status is unknown.
Malpedia associates ELMER with the Danti actor as well. Shared tooling between these clusters has not been resolved.
Secondary blogs claiming activity since 2012, an 'OpTaiwan' link, or DOORJAMB use were not corroborated and were excluded.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): The relevant environment is the Taiwan and Japan government, media, financial and high-tech information space, plus the political-party networks around Taiwanese elections [S1][S6]. STEP 2 (effects): Office documents arriving by email and unpatched Windows endpoints are the main avenue of approach. Compromised legitimate websites hide second-stage delivery [S2][S4]. STEP 3 (adversary model): Political or contact-update themed spear-phish, then Word EPS exploit plus CVE-2015-1701, then IRONHALO download or ELMER HTTP backdoor, then directory and process discovery [S1][S3][S6]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is spear-phishing for espionage against Taiwanese and Japanese political, media and government organizations around significant political events such as elections [S6][S7]. MDCOA is use of the resulting access to US, allied or partner organizations in the region for sustained collection on regional policy during a crisis; this is not observed in sources. Candidate indicators: Word documents carrying embedded EPS content, privilege escalation via CVE-2015-1701 on endpoints, Delphi-compiled HTTP beacons that honor proxy settings, and second-stage downloads from legitimate but compromised websites [S2][S3][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: Track regional political events, such as Taiwanese elections, as triggers for heightened spear-phishing against partner and media organizations [S6]. (2) Authorities: Partner-nation victims (Taiwanese and Japanese organizations) fall outside DoD networks, so information sharing goes through appropriate partner and interagency channels. (3) Mission assurance: Exploitation relied on known Office and Windows vulnerabilities, so patch compliance for document-handling components is a key mitigation [S1][S4]. (4) Coordination: Reporting is old (2015) and vendor-specific. Coordinate with intelligence partners for current activity before assigning APT16 as a named threat in planning.

provenance.importedSummary: Between November 26, 2015, and December 1, 2015, known and suspected China-based APT groups launched several spear-phishing attacks targeting Japanese and Taiwanese organizations in the high-tech, government services, media and financial services industries. Each campaign delivered a malicious Microsoft Word document exploiting the aforementioned EPS dict copy use-after-free vulnerability, and the local Windows privilege escalation vulnerability CVE-2015-1701. The successful exploitation of both vulnerabilities led to the delivery of either a downloader that we refer to as IRONHALO, or a backdoor that we refer to as ELMER.
